title: Enhancing the yield strength of intercritically annealed Q&P steel via bainite-based quenching and partitioning treatment
abstract: Intercritically annealed Q&P steels exhibit good strength-ductility synergies. Unlike fully austenized Q&P steels, intercritically annealed Q&P steels exhibit good ductility but contain a significant amount of ferrite, resulting in a lower yield strength of the material. To address this challenge, we propose a novel short-time isothermal method for bainite-based quenching and partitioning (B-Q&P) treatments to enhance the yield strength. The experimental results indicate that a short-term isothermal bainitic transformation generates a small quantity of preformed bainitic ferrite (PFB), accelerating primary martensite (PM) transformation and enhancing the PM content during the initial quenching stage. Moreover, the B-Q&P treatment significantly refines the retained austenite (RA) and improves its mechanical stability, thus resulting in a more sustained transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) effect. Furthermore, the results reveal that the yield strength increases from 632 MPa in the conventional Q&P sample to 792 MPa in the B270-Q&P sample, representing a ∼25.3 % improvement, the total elongation increased from 22.4 % in the conventional Q&P sample to 24.1 % in the B270-Q&P sample. Additionally, the impact of the bainite-based quenching temperature on the content and transformation kinetics of the primary martensite is examined.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steel, as a representative of third-generation advanced high-strength steel (AHSS), is used in the automobile industry owing to its high strength and ductility [ 1–6 ]. The Q&P steel was first reported by Speer et al., in 2003 [ 7 ]. The Q&P process encompasses several key stages: a full/partial austenitization stage, an initial quenching stage below the martensite start temperature (Ms), then raising the temperature for carbon partitioning and enhancing austenite stability (the partitioning temperature is typically no less than the quenching temperature), and finally quenching to room temperature [ 8–12 ]. Compared to fully austenized Q&P steels, the final microstructure of intercritically annealed Q&P steel contains a large amount of ferrite, which significantly reduces its yield strength [ 13 , 14 ]. Therefore, enhancing the yield strength of intercritically annealed Q&P steels remains a challenge.

To improve the yield strength of intercritically annealed Q&P steel, researchers have [ 15–20 ] investigated the addition of alloy elements such as C, Mn, V, Nb, and Cu. This has resulted in solid solution strengthening, grain refinement strengthening, precipitation strengthening, all of which enhance the yield strength, albeit to a limited extent. The alteration of the heat treatment primarily focuses on three aspects: pre-treatment, the Q&P process, and the Q&PT (tempering) treatment. For the pre-treatment, Gu et al. [ 21 ] found that pre-existing martensite accelerated austenite nucleation, reduced the ferrite content, and enhanced the yield strength by 200 MPa, however, the initial microstructure was a fully martensite microstructure, which is hard to implement in an industry setting. Sun et al. [ 22 ] revealed that pre-quenching refined the microstructure and increased the yield strength by 24 MPa, similar to the results reported by Zhang et al. [ 23 ]. Cheng et al. [ 24 ] discovered that the initial microstructure of cold-rolled steels achieved a higher yield strength compared to that of hot-rolled steels, with an increase of up to ∼150 MPa. In our previous work, a pre-annealing treatment was adopted to improve the bainitic ferrite content, which significantly increased the yield strength of an intercritically annealed Q&P steel from 438 MPa to 821 MPa [ 6 ]. However, the pre-annealing treatment resulted in increased industrial production costs. Regarding the Q&P process, Liu et al. [ 25 ] showed that a fast heating rate significantly raised the austenite content, reduced the ferrite content, and enhanced the yield strength by 90–140 MPa. Meanwhile, Kamikawa et al. [ 26 ] revealed that a fast heating rate refined the final microstructure and improved the yield strength by 30–50 MPa, similar to the results reported by Liu et al. [ 27 ]. With regard to intercritical annealing temperatures and times, researchers [ 25 , 28 ] have found that higher intercritical annealing temperatures or longer annealing times could reduce the ferrite content and enhance the yield strength during the soaking period. Regarding quenching temperatures, Wang et al. [ 29 ] reported that lowering the quenching temperature increased the primary martensite content, thereby significantly improving the yield strength, for instance, the yield strength increased to over 300 MPa when the quenching temperature was reduced from 275 °C to 150 °C, with the latter being particularly low (∼150 °C). For the Q&PT treatment, Rong et al. [ 17 ] found that the tempering treatment in a Cu-containing Q&P steel produced substantial Cu precipitates and increases the yield strength by 130 MPa. In general, previous research has found that an increase in primary martensite (PM) content significantly increases the yield strength of intercritically annealed Q&P steel; therefore, it is crucial to improve the primary martensite content in intercritically annealed Q&P steel.

In recent years, several scholars [ 30–42 ] have proposed a novel method for the pre-isothermal bainitic transformation (PIBT) of bainitic and Q&P steels. The PIBT treatment mainly focuses on isothermal treatment below the bainite start temperature (B S ) to form partial bainite prior to the first quenching stage of Q&P steel or the austempering stage of bainitic steel. For bainitic steels, Avishan et al. [ 30 ] found that PIBT treatment significantly improved the RA stability, reduced the blocks RA content, increased the film-like RA content, and enhanced ductility, which was similar to the results reported by Hase et al. [ 31 ]. Gao et al. [ 32 ] showed that PIBT increased the carbon content in RA and enhanced RA stability. Mousalou et al. [ 33 ] reported that PIBT treatment refined the bainitic size, resulting in an ultrafine bainitic microstructure and a significant increase in impact fracture toughness. Sun et al. [ 34 ] suggested that PIBT could facilitate VC precipitation that refined the bainitic size. Moreover, Ravi reported [ 35 ] that PIBT treatment decorated the parent austenite grain boundaries with grain-boundary cementite prior to bainitic ferrite formation, accelerated bainitic ferrite formation kinetics owing to a decrease in the activation energy for bainitic ferrite nucleation at the cementite/austenite interfaces, and reduced bainitic isothermal time. For Q&P steels, the PIBT treatment was first reported by Gao et al., in 2014 [ 36 ], abbreviated as B-Q&P treatment (bainite-based quenching and partitioning treatment). Furthermore, Gao et al. [ 36–39 ] revealed that the B-Q&P treatment not only refined the ductile matrix but also enhanced the strength, ductility, and toughness simultaneously, similar results were reported by Zhao et al. [ 40 ]. Moreover, Peng et al. [ 41 ] suggested that preformed bainitic ferrite could improve the carbon content in RA, enhanced the RA stability, and achieved excellent mechanical properties. Liu et al. [ 42 ] discovered that the B-Q&P treatment could improve the carbon content in retained austenite and filmy retained austenite. Previous research indicates that B-Q&P mainly focuses on refining the grain size, accelerating the bainitic transformation, and improving the RA stability. However, preformed bainitic ferrite, acting as a second-phase particle, can provide nucleation sites to promote primary martensite transformation, was ignored.

This study proposes a novel method for significantly improving the yield strength of intercritically annealed Q&P steel. Compared with conventional Q&P processes, the effects of preformed bainitic ferrite on the formation of primary martensite and mechanical properties in B-Q&P steel are elucidated. Furthermore, the influence of bainite-based temperature on the phase fractions is revealed.

sections.heading: Materials and processing
paragraphs:
Table 1 
                          lists the chemical composition of the experimental steel in weight percent. To inhibit the formation of cementite, an Si concentration of 1.66 wt % was selected. A low concentration of Al (0.09 wt%) was selected to facilitate oxide removal. Additionally, low concentrations of Nb (0.03 wt%) and Ti (0.03 wt%) were selected to refine the grain size. The A C3  of 865 °C, A C1  of 737 °C, M s  of 284 °C and M f  of 66 °C were measured using a TA Instrument DIL805A/D dilatometer. The alloy ingot was initially cast using a vacuum induction furnace. It was subsequently forged into slabs with dimensions of 210 × 150 × 80 mm and cut into blocks of 150 × 80 × 26 mm. The blocks were subsequently homogenized at 1250 °C for 2 h. They were then hot rolled into plates in seven passes, reducing the thickness from 26 mm to 2.6 mm, and subsequently air-cooled to 580 °C. Next, the plates were placed inside a box furnace set to 580 °C and furnace-cooled to room temperature at a cooling rate of ∼21 °C/h to simulate coiling. Finally, the plates underwent pickling and cold rolling to achieve a thickness of 1.2 mm.

For the Q&P processes, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at 840 °C for 120 s in a box furnace, followed by quenching in a salt bath at a target temperature (270 °C or 240 °C) for 5 s. The sheets were subsequently quenched to 200 °C via oil cooling (the traditional Q&P process involves direct oil cooling to 200 °C). Subsequently, they were austempered in a salt bath at 460 °C for 120 s and finally quenched by water cooling to room temperature. The schematic of the heat treatment can be found in  Fig. 1 
                         . For simplicity, the samples are referred to as Q&P, B240-Q&P, and B270-Q&P in the following sections based on their pre-quenching conditions. The temperature of all the samples was monitored using a K-type thermocouple. All the cold rolled sheets underwent the heat treatment were 120 mm long, 80 mm wide, and 1.2 mm in thickness.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs:
The microstructures were characterized using a Zeiss Ultra-55 field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM). The samples were mechanically ground with sandpaper, polished with 2.5 μm diamond paste, and then etched using a 4 % Nital solution. The volume fraction of retained austenite was measured by X-ray diffraction (XRD) using a Rigaku D/Max 2400 machine with Cu Kα radiation, and the 2θ angle ranged from 40° to 101° with a step size of 2.5°/min. The retained austenite distribution was characterized using a Zeiss Gemini SEM 300 equipped with an Oxford NordlysNano EBSD detector with a step size of 0.05 μm and tilt angle of 70°. The data obtained were analyzed using the Oxford HKL Channel 5 software. The XRD and EBSD samples were mechanically ground and electropolished using an electropolishing solution containing 12.5 vol% perchloric acid in alcohol. The electrolytic polishing parameters were 20 V and 20 s. The microstructural characteristics of the retained austenite were also characterized using an FEI Tecnai G2 F20 transmission electron microscope. The TEM samples were initially prepared as a Φ3 mm foil with thickness of 50 μm, and twin-jet polished using 12.5 % perchloric acid alcohol at −25 °C using a voltage of 30 V.

To quantitatively characterize the content of multiple phases, the ferrite content was calculated using ImagePro Plus software. The volume fractions of the preformed martensite, preformed bainitic ferrite, primary martensite, and bainitic ferrite were calculated using the lever rule based on the heating and cooling curves obtained using a Bahr DIL805A/D dilatometer. The size of the dilatometric samples was 10 × 4 × 1.2 mm, and the volume fraction of fresh martensite was calculated as a balance.

sections.heading: Mechanical testing
paragraphs: Tensile tests were conducted using a SANS CMT-3000 tensile machine with a crosshead speed of 2 mm/min. The size of the tensile sample was 25 mm in gauge length, 6.25 mm in width and 1.2 mm in thickness. The longitudinal axis of the tensile sample was parallel to the rolling direction. The tensile sample surface was pickled and mechanically polished, and three samples from each condition were tested to ensure repeatability of the results.

sections.heading: Microstructure and phase fractions in the B-Q&P samples
paragraphs:
To determine the effect of the B-Q&P treatment on the final microstructures, the final microstructures after different B-Q&P treatments were examined.  Fig. 2 
                          shows that the final microstructure mainly consisted of ferrite (F), primary martensite (PM), bainitic ferrite (BF), final martensite (FM), and retained austenite (RA). Typically, intercritically annealed Q&P steel may form this kind of final microstructure [ 18 , 44 ]. As shown in  Fig. 2 , the ferrite had a size of 1– 4 μm and was uniformly distributed; however, the volume fractions of the ferrite could not be directly obtained via SEM. The volume fractions of ferrite, amounting to 22.3 %, were quantitatively determined using the ImagePro Plus software.

Q&P steels primarily moderate the heat process to improve the RA content and enhance the ductility. To analyze the effect of B-Q&P treatment on RA, the content of RA was characterized by XRD, as shown in  Fig. 3 
                         , the B-Q&P treatment reduced the RA content gradually from 11.7 % in the Q&P sample to 9.3 % in the B270-Q&P sample, as the isothermal temperature increased. Furthermore, the morphology of RA in Q&P steel should not be ignored. To reveal the effect of the B-Q&P treatment on the morphology of RA, combined band contrast and phase maps are presented in  Fig. 4 
                         . Red regions represent RA, while brighter gray regions indicate ferrite. Ferrite appears brighter because it does not have a high defect density. Darker gray regions represent primary martensite and bainitic ferrite, which are not easily distinguishable. The black regions represent fresh martensite, which is full of defects because tempering was not performed [ 6 ]. Compared to the Q&P treatment, the B-Q&P treatment refined the size of the RA, increased the film-like RA content, and reduced the block RA content, which was especially the B270-Q&P sample. The RA content from EBSD results is consistent with previous XRD results. In addition, the majority of RA was distributed along the prior austenite grain boundaries. The effect of the B-Q&P treatment on the stability of RA via EBSD is challenging owing to relationship between RA stability and various factors such as size, morphology, surrounding phase, and carbon concentration [ 29 ]. Compared to the Q&P sample, the effective grain size of the B-Q&P sample exhibited a slight decrease from 0.43 μm in the Q&P sample to 0.27 μm in the B270-Q&P sample, as shown in  Fig. 5 
                         . According to previous research [ 29 , 45 ], a lower quenching temperature improves the PM content and refines RA size. The refined RA experiences minimal martensitic transformation, even under smaller strains. Furthermore, the majority of blocky RA were observed at the prior austenite grain (PAG) boundaries and adjacent to bainitic ferrite and ferrite.

Owing to the resolution limitation of EBSD, it is difficult to characterize RA smaller than 30 nm. Therefore, the nanosized RA of the B270-Q&P sample was further characterized by TEM, as shown in  Fig. 6 
                         . For the B270-Q&P sample, the blocky shaped RA with a size of 100 – 300 nm adjacent to bainitic ferrite is shown in  Fig. 6 (b). The corresponding selected area diffraction (SAD) pattern is shown in  Fig. 6 (c), revealing the presence of film-like RA with a width of 20 – 50 nm between the martensite laths. Twinned martensite can be observed in  Fig. 6 (f), which is mainly attributed to the instability of RA and its transformation into twinned martensite during the final quenching process [ 29 ].

The SEM results show that the B-Q&P treatment increased PM content and decreased BF and FM contents. To investigate the effect of the B-Q&P treatment on the final microstructures, particularly on the phase content, the ferrite was calculated via image analysis, the RA content was measured via XRD, and the preformed bainitic ferrite (PFB), primary martensite (PM), and bainitic ferrite (BF) contents were calculated using dilatometry and the lever rule [ 46–51 ],  Fig. 7 
                          (a) shows the dilatometric curve as a function of temperature. The FM content was calculated as the remainder, and the results are shown in  Fig. 7  (b). Owing to the same annealing temperature and time, the ferrite contents in all the samples were similar (∼22.3 vol %), and the B-Q&P treatment slightly reduced the RA content, from 11.7 % in the Q&P sample to 9.3 % in B270-Q&P sample. This suggests that the B-Q&P treatment had a limited effect on carbon partitioning in austenite in the isothermal stage. However, the B-Q&P treatment significantly improved the PM content, particularly in the B270-Q&P sample, marking a 256 % improvement. Moreover, the higher PFB content may be attributed to the synergistic effect of the bainitic transformational driving force and rate of transformation [ 52 ]. The reason for the improved bainitic ferrite content is explained in detail later. In particular, the B-Q&P treatment significantly reduced the BF and FM contents, especially for the FM, which decreased from 29.2 % in the Q&P sample to 15.0 % in the B270-Q&P sample.

sections.heading: Effect of the B-Q&P treatment on mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The effect of the B-Q&P treatment on the mechanical properties is shown in  Fig. 8 
                         , and the relevant mechanical properties are summarized in  Fig. 8 (b) and  Table 2 
                         . The Q&P sample had the lowest yield strength of 632 MPa. However, the B-Q&P samples exhibited a significant increase in yield strength from 632 MPa for the Q&P sample to 792 MPa for the B270-Q&P sample, indicating an increase of approximately 25.3 %. In addition, the B-Q&P treatment also enhanced the total elongation (TEL) with an increase of approximately 2 %.  Fig. 8  (c) shows the work-hardening behavior of different B-Q&P samples, where the work-hardening curve of the Q&P samples gradually decreased with an increase in the tensile strain. However, clear evidence of the TRIP effect is seen in the upward curvature of the work-hardening curves of the B270-Q&P sample. Moreover, compared to the Q&P sample, the B-Q&P treatment exhibited excellent work-hardening capacity, indicating its superior ductility.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: According to the experimental results, the B-Q&P treatment significantly increased the PM content and enhanced the yield strength. The origins of the enhanced yield strength, as well as the improved PM content, are discussed, and the mechanism and effect of the B-Q&P treatment on PM are revealed in the following sections.

To elucidate the influence of the B-Q&P treatment on the yield strength, the effect of the B-Q&P treatment on PM cannot be neglected. The PFB and FM transformation contents were calculated using the lever rule with heating and cooling curves in  Fig. 7  (a). The cooling and heating processes are indicated using arrows, and the relevant results are shown in  Fig. 9 
                      . During the initial quenching stage, the start of martensite transformation was 285 °C, which is mainly attributed to C and Mn enriched austenite in the intercritical annealing conditions. Moreover, compared to the Q&P sample, the formation of PFB in the B-Q&P samples significantly increased the PM content. Furthermore, the B-Q&P treatment accelerated the PM transformation rate. To investigate the effect of B-Q&P treatment on the PM, a schematic illustrating the microstructural evolution is shown in  Fig. 10 
                      . Before quenching to 200 °C, only the PM is formed in Q&P sample. However, for the B-Q&P samples, owing to the presence of a pre-isothermal stage, a small amount of PFB was formed. These PFBs act as defects and nucleation sites, accelerating the PM transformation. The highest content of PFB in the B270-Q&P sample is mainly attributed to the synergy between the driving force and bainitic transformation rate. The partitioning temperature decreases as the driving force of bainitic transformation gradually increases, thereby accelerating bainitic formation. However, when partitioning below Ms, the untransformed austenite gradually reduces with decreasing the partitioning temperature, resulting in a lower BF transition rate. The synergistic effect of the driving force and transition rate led to the formation of the highest amount of PFB in the B270-Q&P sample [ 52 , 53 ].

Fig. 11 
                       shows the bainite transformation kinetics at the temperature of 460 °C. The Q&P sample exhibited the highest bainitic ferrite content (23.5 %), followed by the B240-Q&P sample with 15.1 %, and the lowest content was observed in the B270-Q&P sample with 13.0 %. The B-Q&P treatment significantly reduced the bainitic ferrite content, which decreased with increasing temperature. The B-Q&P treatment significantly reduced the BF content, which can explain the lower RA content in the B-Q&P sample during the final partitioning stage, particularly in the B270-Q&P sample. Moreover, in the final quenching stage, the FM content of the B-Q&P sample was lower. This was attributed to carbon partitioning from PM into untransformed austenite, which enhanced the stability of austenite. Moreover, the bainitic transformation was nearly completed at an isothermal time of approximately 60 s, which is similar to that reported in the literature [ 52 ]. The dilation curve exhibited a decreasing tend after 60 s. Zhang et al. [ 53 ] attributed this to carbide formation. The B-Q&P treatment improved the PM content, and the solubility of carbon in PM was significantly lower than that in RA and BF. Consequently, the activity and diffusivity of carbon atoms in the B-Q&P sample increased, thereby accelerating the formation and growth of carbides. Carbide formation leads to contraction of the crystal structure during the partitioning process.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
In this study, the influence of bainite-based quenching and partitioning on the microstructure and mechanical properties of an intercritically annealed Q&P steel was investigated. Bainite-based quenching resulted in a small amount of PFB, which promoted primary martensite transformation, increased the primary martensite content, and significantly enhanced the yield strength. The main conclusions are as follows: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            Prior isothermal bainitic transformation treatment can form a small amount of preformed bainitic ferrite, and the content of preformed bainitic ferrite increased gradually with an increase in quenching temperature, from 0 % for the Q&P sample to 5.3 % for the B270-Q&P sample. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            As nucleation sites, PFB can accelerate the primary martensite transformation and significantly improve the primary martensite content in the initial quenching stage. The PM content increased from 13.3 % in the Q&P sample to 35.1 % in the B270-Q&P sample, representing an improvement of ∼264 %. Additionally, the B-Q&P process refined the size of RA because it increased PM content and film-like RA between the martensite laths. The size of RA decreased from 0.43 μm in the Q&P sample to 0.27 μm in the B270-Q&P sample. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            B-Q&P treatment significantly improved the primary martensite content, thereby reducing bainitic ferrite and final martensite contents. In particular, the FM content decreased from 29.2 % in the Q&P sample to 15.0 % in the B270-Q&P sample. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            A higher primary martensite content resulted in a significant increase in the yield strength of the B-Q&P sample. The yield strength improved from 632 MPa (Q&P) to 792 MPa (B270-Q&P), representing a ∼20 % improvement. The B-Q&P treatment resulted in a more sustained TRIP effect and enhanced the work-hardening capacity. The TEL improved from 22.4 % in the Q&P sample to 24.1 % in the B270-Q&P sample.

paragraphs: The raw/processed data required to reproduce these findings cannot be shared at this time as they also form part of an ongoing study.
